name: Political Advertising Regulation
evidence_rating: ex-ante only, with an early unintended effect: largest platforms withdrew from political ads
summary: The Commission expected EU-wide rules to make political ads more transparent and easier to run across borders, but put no numbers on it. When the rules took effect in October 2025, Google and Meta stopped selling political and social-issue ads in the EU altogether rather than comply, so the regulation's main early effect has been to shrink online political advertising rather than make it more transparent; no study yet measures effects on campaigns or voters.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement contains no indicators section; the Commission will evaluate within two years after each European Parliament election, using contractor data collection

indicators.indicator: Labelled political ads with sponsor, cost and targeting information; common ad repository; better oversight
indicators.evidence: Regulation applies from 10 October 2025. Google (Nov 2024 announcement) and Meta (from 6 Oct 2025) stopped selling political, electoral and social-issue ads in the EU rather than comply, so the main online channels and their ad libraries for such ads have largely disappeared. Pre-application audit found Meta met 9 and Google 7 of 19 transparency criteria in the 2024 EU elections.

indicators.objective: Single market for political advertising services
indicators.indicator: Less fragmentation, lower costs for cross-border campaigns and SMEs scaling up
indicators.evidence: Not measured; the exit of the largest platforms points the other way for online services.

indicators.indicator: Restrictions on targeting using personal data

literature.citation: European Commission (2021), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on the transparency and targeting of political advertising (executive summary SWD(2021) 356), SWD(2021) 355
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on the transparency and targeting of political advertising (executive summary SWD(2021) 356)
literature.headline: Expected more legal certainty and lower fragmentation costs, transparency of targeting, better oversight and public trust; compliance costs offset by efficiency gains; no quantified headline
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected clearer, EU-wide rules to make political ads more transparent and cheaper to run across borders, but gave no figures.

literature.citation: Meyer et al. (European Digital Media Observatory) (2025), A Cross-Country Analysis of Electoral Advertising on Meta and Google during the EU 2024 Elections: Compliance, Transparency, and Targeting, EDMO report, September 2025
literature.authors: Meyer et al. (European Digital Media Observatory)
literature.title: A Cross-Country Analysis of Electoral Advertising on Meta and Google during the EU 2024 Elections: Compliance, Transparency, and Targeting
literature.method: descriptive audit of ad libraries across 15 Member States (before the Regulation applied)
literature.headline: Meta and Google definitions not fully aligned with Regulation 2024/900; Meta met 9 and Google 7 of 19 transparency criteria; about 30,000 ads and EUR 8.7m spent by parties in 15 countries; targeting common but mostly broad; Meta targeting details disappearing by Aug 2025
literature.summary_plain: Before the rules applied, an audit of the 2024 EU election found Meta and Google only partly met the new transparency standards, with parties spending about EUR 8.7 million on 30,000 ads in 15 countries.

literature.citation: Meta (2025), Ending Political, Electoral and Social Issue Advertising in the EU in Response to Incoming European Regulation, Meta Newsroom, 25 July 2025 (updated 6 October 2025)
literature.title: Ending Political, Electoral and Social Issue Advertising in the EU in Response to Incoming European Regulation
literature.headline: From 6 October 2025 Meta no longer delivers political, electoral and social-issue ads in the EU, citing 'unworkable requirements and legal uncertainties' of the Regulation; notes other platforms have done the same
literature.summary_plain: Meta stopped all political and social-issue ads in the EU in October 2025, blaming the new rules; Google had already announced the same in 2024.
literature.interested_party: Regulated company; statement explains its own commercial decision

literature.authors: MedDMO (Mediterranean Digital Media Observatory; researchers incl. Sirivianos, M. and Andreou, A., Cyprus University of Technology)
literature.title: Anonymous third-party paid political advertising in the Cyprus 2026 parliamentary elections
literature.method: systematic monitoring of paid political content in Meta, Google and TikTok ad libraries/APIs (machine-learning search on 753 candidate and party names) from the TTPA application date
literature.outcomes: political ads sold despite platform bans; anonymous sponsors; enforcement
literature.headline: Five anonymous advertising operations ran more than 450 political ads in the final weeks of the campaign, and platform enforcement was largely reactive, after ads had reached large audiences.
literature.summary_plain: After the EU's political-ad rules took effect and Meta and Google said they would stop selling political ads, researchers in Cyprus still found hundreds of election ads, some from anonymous sponsors spreading fake polls.
literature.quality: Systematic measurement but single small election; detailed figures (e.g. 2,457 Meta ads, 887 TikTok ads) only via secondary report (Tech Policy Press); landing page read
literature.citation: MedDMO (Mediterranean Digital Media Observatory; researchers incl. Sirivianos, M. and Andreou, A., Cyprus University of Technology) (2026), Anonymous third-party paid political advertising in the Cyprus 2026 parliamentary elections, EDMO / MedDMO publication, 2026

literature.title: What Data Reveals About Meta and Google's Political Ad Ban in the EU
literature.method: descriptive analysis of TTPA self-disclosures on the Dutch politiekereclame.nl portal (65 campaigns) plus Meta Ad Library spending data
literature.outcomes: quality of TTPA transparency disclosures; loss of ad-library data
literature.headline: Of 65 Dutch election campaigns tracked under TTPA self-reporting, only 43 (66%) reported which media channels they used; the three largest without channel data represented over EUR 3.2m in spending.
literature.summary_plain: A researcher looked at the first disclosures political advertisers made under the new EU rules in the Dutch election and found them patchy and unstandardised, while Meta and Google's exit removed the main public ad archives.
literature.period_geography: Oct 2025; Netherlands (plus EU Meta spending since 2022)
literature.quality: Small descriptive sample inside an opinion piece by an academic; early, one election
literature.citation: Votta, F. (2025), What Data Reveals About Meta and Google's Political Ad Ban in the EU, Tech Policy Press (commentary)
